newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, Indonesia agree on anti-terrorist stand.
newsitem.headline: Japan, Indonesia agree on anti-terrorist stand.

text.p: Indonesian President Suharto and Japanese Premier Ryutaro Hashimoto, whose country is mired in a hostage crisis in Peru, agreed on Thursday that terrorism must be opposed or the pattern of violence would continue.
Hashimoto arrived in Jakarta from Kuala Lumpur for a three-day visit and talks with Suharto were expected to cover bilateral, regional and global issues.
Indonesia's State Secretary Murdiono said the issue of terrorism was raised at a courtesy meeting between the two men after Suharto formally welcomed Hashimoto at the state palace in central Jakarta.

"Both leaders agreed we must not give in to terrorism, because if the demands of terrorists were met, this would become a pattern and lead to similar demands in the future," Murdiono told reporters after a brief meeting between the two leaders.

Hashimoto is being accompanied by a task force with communications equipment to keep him in constant contact with Tokyo and Peru, where Marxist rebels are holding hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
Murdiono said it was important for the international community to act to prevent crises like the one in Peru.
"President Suharto expressed his hope that the hostage crisis in Peru can be overcome as well as possible," he added.

Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels stormed the the Japanese ambassador's residence on December 17 and took about 500 hostages including ambassadors and senior Peruvian government officials. The majority have since been released.
Murdiono also said Hashimoto expressed Japan's intention to expand its ties with the seven-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) beyond purely economic interests.
On his current trip, Hashimoto is visiting ASEAN members Brunei, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam and Singapore. He visited the group's other two members, Thailand and the Philippines, last year.

Thursday's schedule in Jakarta was largely ceremonial. The Japanese leader was laying a wreath at the Kalibata cemetery where Indonesia's national heros are buried and planting a tree at a park in east Jakarta.
Suharto was to host an official dinner in the evening.

The leaders will hold substantive talks on Friday but Hashimoto will avoid contentious issues such as Indonesia's controversial national car policy and human rights in East Timor, Japanese Ambassador Taizo Watanabe told a pre-arrival briefing.
He said Hashimoto believed "maintaining and cementing close cooperation and foreign relations with Indonesia is vitally important".
He noted Japan was Indonesia's biggest trading partner and biggest aid donor. Japanese investment in Indonesia rose to nearly $7.0 billion in 1996 from $3.8 billion in 1995.
Indonesia, the largest Southeast Asian country with a population of 200 million, is Japan's third-largest foreign source of oil and natural gas.
Fifty-three percent of Japan's vital raw material imports move through the sea lanes of the Indonesian archipelago.
